Not stubborn, but disappointing
Aug 2026 • Friends
We have dined at Stubborn Seed every year during Miami Spice, and until this year it had been one of our favorite restaurants. Unfortunately, our third visit was a major disappointment.

The $65 Miami Spice menu simply did not deliver the value or quality we have come to expect from a Michelin-starred restaurant. The corn panna cotta appetizer was literally the size of an amuse-bouche gone in two bites.

For the main course, we both ordered the lamb. It arrived as two paper-thin slices of lamb accompanied by just a few grilled vegetables. The entire plate was the size of what many restaurants would serve as a small appetizer. While the presentation was attractive, the portion was so minimal that it felt more like a tasting sample than a main course.

Dessert was equally disappointing. It was described as a panna cotta, but what arrived was a tiny sliver of cake with a bit of citrus and a single shard of meringue. It bore little resemblance to a traditional panna cotta and was an underwhelming finish to the meal.

We understand that fine dining emphasizes quality over quantity, but both were lacking here. The portions were exceptionally small, and the overall quality of the dishes was mediocre and well below what we expect from a Michelin-starred restaurant. There was nothing about this menu that justified either the price or the restaurant’s reputation.

After three consecutive years of visiting, this was a surprising decline. There are simply too many outstanding restaurants participating in Miami Spice to spend $65 per person on a menu that leaves you disappointed and still hungry. Based on this experience, we cannot recommend the Miami Spice menu at Stubborn Seed, and unfortunately, after three years of supporting the restaurant, we will not be returning.

Barren Seed
May 2026 • Friends
For a milestone birthday I wanted to go with something that represented living vicariously through the life of someone who attained a career I once dreamed of. Not saying I'm unhappy at all with my career, but most people who know me also know from early on I aspired to become a renowned chef. Limitations at the time didn't make that possible, but the culinary arts remain a core part of who I am. Entered how impressed we were last year with the Miami Spice menu that on the spot I selected Stubborn Seed as the venue for my milestone birthday. Enter a process, meal, and aftermath made to the horror model of movies like Sinners.

Let me start with the reservation. I booked in October 2025 to ensure we would have the place booked for my birthday. At the time we had a placeholder menu which we would adjust closer to the date. I was told then the 6 course menu would not be available. Closer to the date I saw on the website the 6 course menu was indeed available. In reaching out to the team member who took my reservation and contract, she told me the 6 course menu was not available on Fridays. From what you can see in the pictures, it was available. Then we wonder why Miami gets the reputation it does,..

...finally we settled on the 6 course meny after all. My party showed up and we had a great time. Most courses were really solid. Notable was the first course, the cured Ginger & Citrus Cured Japanese Yellowtail. Everything kept moving in a definite crescendo until the let down of the main course. The Koji Marinated Lamb Loin was better billed as the "mini loin" as it was indeed incredibly small. I considered summoning Avenger level superpowers to reduce my people in size to the Wasp to make this work somehow. Unfortunately I don't possess such superpowers. If only. But that was not all. Wait for it...

...There was not one single acknowledgment by anyone in the restaurant staff about my milestone birthday. Not a thank you for selecting us. Not a mention by the manager or anyone on the staff. Not even a gesture during dessert. Even the most elegant of restaurants do something. Even a plated decoration acknowledging the occasion would have sufficed. I wasn't asking for Longhorn Steakhouse staff type of fanfare but something would have been adequate. Nothing. But wait, there's more...

...when settling the check I mentioned I had prepaid for the 10 tasting menus ahead of time leaving on premises consumption for payment on site. At the restaurante they looked into it and came back with that the prepayment was never charged. Given I was with my guests that was neither the time nor the place, so I settled the bill with the intent on checking this later. I did and they had indeed double charged me $2,000. Needless to say I had to bring this up to them including opening a dispute with my credit card after days went by without a follow up on where my refund stood. No offense ladies and gentlemen, but this mistake should have never taken place in the first place...

All in all, not even they have the power to ruin what was one of the most memorable evenings of my life. Why? because I was surrounded by some of the most amazing human beings who took time to share this birthday with me. I love them and am grateful to have them in my life. That was the main event. The hopes was having a similar amazing experience with the meal at Stubborn Seed would be the icing on the case. It was not. Fortunately for me they didn't add anything, but more importantly, they didn't take anything away. That said, since Michelin doesn't judge a restaurant for portion size or service, I thought I myself would take something away - the veil on a restaurant that is evidently self indulgent and does not and will not care about you. You are not the star, and you never will be.

A Refined Culinary Journey at Stubborn Seed
May 2025 • Couples
A Refined Culinary Journey at Stubborn Seed 

Exquisite Service Sets the Stage 
From the moment we stepped inside, Stubborn Seed’s Michelin-starred hospitality shone through. Arturo—a dedicated four-year veteran—ensured every detail was attended to with precision, creating a welcoming atmosphere that elevated the entire experience. 

The Spring Tasting Menu—A Masterclass in Execution 

The evening opened with a bread course featuring seasoned whipped feta and ornamental baby carrots—a simple yet flavorful introduction that set a refined tone for what was to come. 

Next, the Nagasaki Prefecture Sashimi arrived, showcasing Bluefin tuna delicately paired with soy milk, blueberry, and vanilla. This dish presented a subtle interplay of umami and sweetness that gently prepped the palate. 

Immediately following, a finger food box presentation introduced three artfully crafted bites: 
- Enhanced Caviar Cream Macaron – An indulgent, airy confection elevated by a hint of salty sophistication. 
- Wagyu Tartare – A bright, refined blend of aged soy, sesame, apple, shiso, wasabi, and chive oil, offering bold umami with a refreshing crispness. 
- Sungold Tomato Pâte de Fruit – A playful balance of milk bread, kumquat gel, papaya & radish kimchi, and crispy lard that encapsulated sweetness paired with layered acidity. 

This trio served as a creative interlude—a nod to both artistry and high-end flavor in a compact format. 

The progression continued with the Hudson Valley Foie Gras Torchon. While not the most memorable course, it distinguished itself through originality and sophistication, artfully balanced with kumquat gel and lard. 

Following was the Confit Duck Cappelletti, where the notes of fennel, orange, and black garlic, accented by a subtle rosemary gel, delivered a layered, complex taste that exemplified meticulous seasoning. 

The intermezzo—a masterful heirloom tomato consommé—proved to be the best bite of the night for my wife. Its pure, concentrated essence captured the season’s vibrancy and offered a palate-cleansing brilliance. 

Then came the Striped Sea Bass, my personal standout. Its luxuriously tender texture was perfectly enhanced by a saffron-infused tomato gel, with delicate hints of zucchini and a whisper of chili threads providing a balanced, multifaceted depth. 

The Enchotan-Seared Florida Oyster, enhanced by tallow, introduced a surprising Texas BBQ essence that brilliantly contrasted with its inherent brininess, melding smokiness and freshness in a harmonious duet. 

The final savory course showcased a bold twist: the Dry-Aged Cacio e Pepe Australian Wagyu Beef. This enhancement replaced the original lamb dish, merging the richness of dry-aging with the bold, peppery notes of Cacio e Pepe. The result was an intense umami experience, where creamy, pepper-infused accents elevated the melt-in-your-mouth beef to new heights. 

Desserts & Wine Pairings—A Grand Finale 

For dessert, the Cortexa Reverie staged a brilliant finale. This inventive creation blended miso panna cotta with lively notes of passion fruit and mango—enhanced by a mango passion fruit gel, crowned with a white chocolate passion fruit crumble, and accompanied by a refreshing toasted corn ice cream. 

The wine selections further amplified the experience. The G.D. Vajra Moscato d'Asti provided a perfectly balanced pairing—neither too sweet nor too dry—ideal for the lighter courses. Meanwhile, the Alto Moncayo Garnacha lent deep richness to the umami-driven bites, and the Contrada Monte Gorna Etna Rosso delivered a volcano of minerality that beautifully complemented the smoked elements of the meal. 

Conclusion—A Michelin Experience Worth Every Moment 

Every component of this tasting menu—from the innovative flavors and meticulous techniques to Arturo’s impeccable, attentive service—reinforced Stubborn Seed’s Michelin star status. The enhanced caviar detail, the ingenious wine pairings, and the flawless execution across a spectrum of dishes create a culinary narrative that is both daring and refined. Truly, this was a meal worth savoring—each bite crafted to perfection.

This meant this restaurant is really not suited to a quiet romantic evening at all: you can't even keep a conversation without raising your voices and sometimes need to shout in the ear of the service. Despite that, the service from Axl (Matthew) was phenomenal--perfect balance between warm friendliness and expert professionalism: he guided us through the plates and pairings. We chose the Tasting Menu (although 3 hours is very difficult in deafening acoustics), and the wine pairing. The 9 courses of food on the menu was fair (warm celery root) very good (lamb, Asian lavish bread) to excellent (lobster) to mind-blowing (cobia) : no real fails, but some suggestions for improvement are due. 
Suggestions:
The celery root dish: I found the puck of warm celery root braised with herbes de Provence and some lemon needs to be changed. The chef treats the root like meat, pairing it with slivers of maitake mushrooms crisped in tempura batter and served with a frothy mustard sauce spiked with Tabasco and quail egg on top. I say the preparation of the celery does not make sense: it seemed simply boiled, the cooking seeming to remove the wildness of the celeriac, and I am stubbornly convinced that it is better to grate the raw celeriac through a coarse Microplane grater and bind it with mayonnaise or cream, adding some nuts, in dish, Cue Iggy's Raw power. The rest of the dish can remain the same.
Next dish up for criticism:
The charred foie gras. I know that this is supposed to be a riff on Katz Delicatessen's Pastrami sandwich (a legendary accomplishment no doubt), but the foie gras was way over-charred, and you lose a lot when you season foie gras to simulate a pastrami. 
The Asian bread lavash was excellent: a chewy, pliable, pita-like round, with an ultrasmooth, ultrarich chicken liver mousse punched up with onion and bourbon and whipped with a dose of butter. Very nice.
Delicate butter poached Maine lobster with ginger and lemongrass-infused green curry foam with bites of bitter garlic and see-through fans of cauliflower. Again, very, very nice.
Jojo Tea Cured Cobia, with the cara cara, spicy celery broth, compressed radish. Best dish of the evening. So well balanced, so delicious. You can make a career from this one plate. I forget which wine Axl paired this with (Spanish white?) but the pairing was absolutely perfect. Keep on stocking that wine. 
Desserts were forgettable, sorry. They did not seem up to the quality of the main dishes. 
For now, it is between Alter and Stubborn Seed if you want to be at the forefront of new Miami cooking. 
I would have liked to have met Chef Jeremy Ford, but it seemed he was wearing an arm sling by end of evening, a little injured. I will be back. Nice if you turn down the volume next time, you do not need it.

The food is very good and foodie-interesting. The prices are high. Our server, happily, was quite knowledgeable about the small menu. We selected two small plates and a large plate to share. We hadn't realized the restaurant subscribed to the "sharing" method until we got there. But, in order to ward off the uncomfortable service we'd had as a couple in "sharing" restaurants before, we were frank with our waiter. We said we didn't care which small plate came first, but the main thing is that there were only two of us and we did not want all three dishes to show up at once. He said the standard thing that is said in all these restaurants: Basically, your food will come out when the chef feels like cooking it. But, he said, he would try to work it so that things came out in a more orderly fashion.

The warm celery root with dijon cream swiftly arrived, and it was delicious. Portions here are not huge, and you are sharing, so generally speaking, you take small bites, savor them, dip them in the cream, try the root with the excellent maitake mushrooms, etc. We weren't even halfway through that when the large plate snapper, also warm, showed up. Before room had even been made on the table (a small two-top) for that, a server was behind the snapper man, holding our small plate of foie gras. When he set that down, he took off a glass top on the plate and a cloud of steam rushed out. Perfectly cooked at perfect temperature, we assumed this was to indicate.

Our server tried to take the blame for this avalanche upon himself. He said he tried to hold off ordering everything, but it just didn't work out. We didn't want him to suffer so we were just going to plow through everything at record speed before it got cold. But then we thought -- at $28 for a 1x2.5-inch piece of foie gras, why were we rushing? We called over a manager and asked to have the foie gras taken back while we enjoyed the other dishes, and that it should be re-delivered when we were ready to eat it.

After the first two dishes were cleared away, it was about 20 minutes before the foie gras reappeared, which was just fine. We had a bottle of wine to keep us happy. The foie gras arrived in another cloud of steam, and we found it delicious, with a unique smokiness. (But let's face it, this was indeed the smallest piece of foie gras we've ever seen, and we tend to order it when we spot it on a menu.) It had a couple of things in which to dip each bite; one I believe was flakes of almond. We enjoyed trying those flavors.

We had asked to see the dessert menu in advance, and we had saved room for the corn pavlova. We love pavlova and have eaten it all over NZ, marveling at how each one is completely different. This one was a bit deconstructed, and it was delicious.

The restaurant ambience is pleasant, and tho the place was full, we could still hear each other talk in the front of the restaurant, where we were seated at a line of two-tops in front of the bar. The wine list was quite reasonably priced. Though the Esk Valley NZ sauvignon we ordered was no longer available, the Albarino we ended up with for $42 was quite good. This price category is much appreciated. The row of two-tops is against a banquette along the window. We couldn't both sit on the banquette because it would have been crowded with the mother-daughter sitting next to us (who were close enough that we ended up chatting with them anyway). But it's the little chair-stool that one of us had to sit in that the restaurant might want to rethink. Not only is it small and uncomfortable, the swiveling seat moves with every body movement.

With two cappuccinos, our bill was about $200. While the casual sharing trend is often said to have originated in tapas bars in Spain and izakayas in Japan, the Stubborn Seed is not a bar where you pound down some olives and tiny fishes and charcuterie with your coworkers over beers. It is a fine-dining restaurant where the staff wants you to enjoy each dish and each flavor. Why make it so hard to do just that?
